passage: In the village school near Sangli, the Class 5 teacher held up Disha's notebook. "Not one sum done. Again. Stand up." Disha stood, her face going red, and stared at her feet. Two rows behind her, Anand felt his own ears burn. He looked down at his slate as if he were the one standing. His stomach turned over, and he pressed his toes hard into the floor. Some boys sniggered. Anand didn't. He wanted to disappear under the bench. When the teacher finally said "Sit," Anand let out a breath he hadn't known he was holding. At recess he walked beside Disha to the tap without saying a word.

qa.q: How many sums had Disha done?
qa.a: Not one sum.

qa.q: Why did Anand's ears burn when it was Disha being scolded?
qa.a: Anand felt Disha's shame as if it were his own, feeling her embarrassment right in his body.

qa.q: At recess Anand walked beside Disha in silence. Why might that small choice matter?
qa.a: It showed Disha she wasn't alone or looked down on, which may have eased the shame more than words.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt hearing the sniggering?
qa.a: Disha probably felt even more humiliated, which makes Anand's quiet company afterwards mean more.

grounding: A boy squirms and looks down when his friend is scolded in class, feeling her shame as his own.

passage: In Year 5 at the primary school in Bristol, Mr Carter stopped the lesson. "Hana, that's the third time you've been talking. Stand up and tell everyone what's so funny." Hana stood. Her voice came out tiny: "Nothing, sir." Across the table, Nkechi's cheeks went hot. She slid lower in her chair and stared at a knot in the wooden desk. Her hands were sweating as if she had been caught. She wanted to cover her ears so she wouldn't hear the silence. When Mr Carter finally turned back to the board, Nkechi slid Hana a note under the pencil case: a small drawing of a cat holding a sign that said IT'S OK.

qa.q: What did Mr Carter tell Hana to do?
qa.a: Stand up and tell everyone what's so funny.

qa.q: Why were Nkechi's hands sweating as if caught?
qa.a: Nkechi was feeling Hana's embarrassment as her own, squirming as though she were the one being called out.

qa.q: How might Hana feel finding the cat note?
qa.a: Hana would probably feel a little less alone and embarrassed, and grateful to Nkechi. 🙂

passage: At the Saturday dance class in the community hall, Guru Maa stopped the music. "Lakshmi, left foot! We have done this step fifty times. Are you even listening?" Everyone froze. Lakshmi's face crumpled, and she stood very still in the middle of the floor. In the back row, Bidisha's whole body went hot. She looked down at her own ankle bells, as if she had missed the step. Her throat tightened. She couldn't look at Lakshmi, and she couldn't look away either. When the music started again, Bidisha danced badly, stiff and out of time. After class, she found Lakshmi tying her shoes and sat down next to her. "That was horrible," Bidisha whispered. "I felt it too."

qa.a: In the community hall.

qa.a: Bidisha felt Lakshmi's embarrassment as if it were her own, with her body going hot and her throat tightening.

qa.q: How might Guru Maa see Bidisha dancing badly after the scolding?

passage:
I'm Jahnavi. My tuition is in Chitra Aunty's flat, eight of us round her dining table. On Tuesday she held up Monu's notebook and said loudly, "Monu, this is copied. From whom?" Monu went red and pressed his lips together.
But the one I noticed was Rafiq. He sits next to me, and he isn't even Monu's best friend, just his cycle friend. He started wriggling on his chair like it was hot. He pulled his sleeves over his hands and bent so low his nose almost touched his book. When Chitra Aunty looked around, Rafiq flinched as if it was his name.
After tuition I asked him, "Why were you hiding? You didn't copy." He kicked a stone. "I know. But my face went hot. It felt like she was saying it to me." Then he went to wait for Monu at the gate.

qa.q: Where does Jahnavi's tuition happen?
qa.a: It is in Chitra Aunty's flat, round her dining table.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel while Monu was being scolded, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt Monu's shame in his own body; he wriggled, hid his hands in his sleeves, bent low and flinched, and later said his face went hot as if it was said to him.

qa.q: What choice does Rafiq make after tuition, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: He goes to wait for Monu at the gate, turning the uncomfortable feeling he shared into company for a friend who may feel alone.

qa.q: How might Monu feel when he finds Rafiq waiting at the gate?
qa.a: Monu may feel less alone and less ashamed, knowing a friend stayed with him instead of keeping away after he was called out.

grounding: It shows a child squirming and hiding when a friend is called out in class, feeling the friend's shame in his own body.

passage:
Monday. At PE, Sir blew his whistle. "Tanuja! No shoes again? Sit on the side." Tanuja sat on the step, her face down. On the track, Nikita's stomach twisted. She ran her lap badly, hot all over, as if Sir had shouted at her.
Wednesday. Sir scolded Tanuja again, for talking in the line. Nikita stared at her own shoes and wished the ground would open, even though she had been quiet the whole time.
Friday. At lunch, Nikita sat by Tanuja under the neem tree. "When Sir shouts at you, I go hot too," she said. "Like it's me."
Tanuja looked up. "Really? I thought everyone was laughing."
"Nobody was laughing," Nikita said. She broke her paratha in half and held one piece out.

qa.q: Where did Nikita and Tanuja sit on Friday?
qa.a: They sat under the neem tree at lunch.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel on Wednesday even though she had done nothing wrong?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and wished the ground would open, as if the scolding were aimed at her, even though she had been quiet the whole time.

qa.q: What changed on Friday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nikita chose to sit with Tanuja and tell her how she felt; putting her hot, shamed feeling into words showed Tanuja that someone was on her side.

qa.q: What does Tanuja reveal about how the scoldings felt to her?
qa.a: Tanuja thought everyone was laughing at her, so hearing Nikita's words lets her see that at least one classmate was feeling it with her instead.

grounding: It shows a child feeling Tanuja's shame in her own body each time Tanuja is scolded, and then sharing that feeling with Tanuja.
